modern:
“Ye *are* Christ’s.” You’re his as a gift, because the Father gave you to the Son. You’re his because he bought you with his blood, counting out the price to set you free. You’re his by dedication, because you’ve given yourself to him. And you’re his by family, because you bear his name and he has made you one of his brothers and sisters and an heir alongside him. Work hard to show the world in practical ways that you’re the servant, the friend, the bride of Jesus.

When you’re tempted to sin, answer, “I cannot do this great wickedness, for I am Christ’s.” Undying principles forbid Christ’s friend to sin. When there’s wealth to be won, if only you’ll sin to get it, say that you’re Christ’s, and don’t touch it. Are you facing hardship and danger? Stand firm in the evil day, remembering that you’re Christ’s. Are you somewhere others are sitting around idle, doing nothing? Get up and work with everything you’ve got. And when the sweat stands on your forehead and you’re tempted to slack off, cry out, “No, I cannot stop, for I am Christ’s. If I were not purchased by blood, I might be like Issachar, crouching between two burdens; but I am Christ’s, and cannot loiter.” When the siren song of pleasure tries to lure you off the right path, answer, “Thy music cannot charm me; I am Christ’s.”

When God’s cause calls you, give away your goods and yourself, because you’re Christ’s. Never let your life contradict what you say you believe. Always be one of those whose manners are Christian, whose speech is like the Nazarene’s, and whose behavior and way of life are so fragrant with heaven that everyone who sees you can tell you belong to the Savior, because they recognize in you his loving features and his holy face. “I am a Roman!” was once a reason for honesty. How much more, then, let this be your reason for holiness: “I am Christ’s!”

notes.note: A gift. Jesus calls his people “the men which thou gavest me” ([[John.17.6|John 17:6]]).
Heirs together with Christ, sharing his inheritance ([[Rom.8.17|Romans 8:17]]).
Joseph’s answer to Potiphar’s wife: “how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” ([[Gen.39.9|Genesis 39:9]]).
A time of trouble and attack. “Take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day” ([[Eph.6.13|Ephesians 6:13]]).
Jacob’s blessing pictures his son Issachar as a strong donkey “couching down between two burdens,” who settles for comfort and ends up a servant ([[Gen.49.14-Gen.49.15|Genesis 49:14–15]]).
In Greek legend the Sirens sang so sweetly that sailors steered toward them and were wrecked.
Contradict what you claim to believe. A “profession” is a public claim to be a Christian.
Jesus, who grew up in Nazareth.
In older English, your whole way of life, not only your talk.
Fragrant with; strongly suggesting.
Roman citizenship was a proud claim that carried rights and a standard to live up to. Paul claimed it in [[Acts.22.25-Acts.22.28|Acts 22:25–28]].

modern:
We shouldn’t go looking for publicity for our goodness or fame for our zeal. But at the same time it’s a sin to be always hiding what God has given us for the good of others. A Christian isn’t meant to be a village tucked away in a valley, but “a city set upon a hill.” We’re not to be a candle hidden under a basket, but a candle on a candlestick, giving light to everyone. Keeping out of sight can be lovely in its season, and hiding yourself is no doubt modest. But hiding *Christ* in us can never be justified, and keeping back truth that is precious to us is a sin against others and an offense against God.

If you’re nervous by temperament and shy by nature, be careful not to give in to this trembling tendency too much, or you’ll be useless to the church. In the name of the One who wasn’t ashamed of you, do a little violence to your feelings, and tell others what Christ has told you. If you can’t speak with a voice like a trumpet, use the still small voice. If the pulpit isn’t to be your platform, and the printing press won’t carry your words on its wings, you can still say with Peter and John, “Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee.” If you can’t preach a sermon on the mountain, talk to the Samaritan woman by Sychar’s well. Speak the praises of Jesus in the house, if not in the temple; in the field, if not on the stock exchange; in your own household, if you can’t in the great family of humanity. From the hidden springs inside you, let sweet little streams of testimony flow out, giving a drink to everyone who passes by. Don’t hide your talent; trade with it, and you’ll bring good interest back to your Lord and Master. Speaking for God will refresh us, cheer the saints, help sinners and honor the Savior. Children who can’t speak are a grief to their parents. Lord, loosen the tongues of all your children.

notes.note: Go looking for attention.
Jesus’ words to his followers in [[Matt.5.14-Matt.5.15|Matthew 5:14–15]], along with the candle not hidden “under a bushel.” A bushel was a large basket used to measure grain.
Keeping out of public view, not stopping work.
Tendency, natural leaning.
How God spoke to Elijah, not in the wind or the earthquake or the fire ([[1Kgs.19.12|1 Kings 19:12]]).
A raised platform for speaking.
Peter’s words to the lame man at the temple gate, just before he healed him ([[Acts.3.6|Acts 3:6]]).
Where Jesus talked one to one with the Samaritan woman ([[John.4.5-John.4.7|John 4:5–7]]).
The stock exchange, where merchants did business.
In Jesus’ parable, a large sum of money a master left with his servants to trade with ([[Matt.25.14-Matt.25.30|Matthew 25:14–30]]).
Small streams.

modern: Solomon’s ships had come home safely, but Jehoshaphat’s never reached the land of gold. Providence makes one man prosper and frustrates another’s plans, in the same business and at the same place, yet the Great Ruler is just as good and wise one time as the other. As we remember this text today, may we have grace to bless the Lord for ships broken at Ezion-geber as well as for ships loaded with earthly blessings. Let’s not envy people who do better than we do, or grumble at our losses as if we alone were singled out for trouble. Like Jehoshaphat, we may be precious in the Lord’s sight even when our plans end in disappointment.

The hidden cause of Jehoshaphat’s loss is well worth noticing, because it’s at the root of a great deal of the suffering of the Lord’s people. It was his alliance with a sinful family, his partnership with sinners. In [[2Chr.20.37|2 Chronicles 20:37]] we’re told that the Lord sent a prophet to declare, “Because thou hast joined thyself with Ahaziah, the Lord hath broken thy works.” This was a father’s discipline, and it seems to have done him good, because in the verse right after our morning’s text we find him refusing to let his servants sail in the same ships as the wicked king’s men. If only Jehoshaphat’s experience would warn the rest of the Lord’s people not to be unequally yoked together with unbelievers! A life of misery is usually the lot of those who bind themselves to the people of the world, in marriage or in any other partnership of their own choosing. Oh, for such love to Jesus that, like him, we may be holy, harmless, undefiled and separate from sinners! If it isn’t like that with us, we can expect to hear it said again and again, *“The Lord hath broken thy works.”*

notes.note: Large ocean-going trading ships, named after Tarshish, a distant port. Solomon’s fleet had brought back gold from Ophir ([[1Kgs.9.26-1Kgs.9.28|1 Kings 9:26–28]]).
A port at the northern tip of the Red Sea, on the Gulf of Aqaba.
God’s care and control over everything that happens, providing for his people.
Loaded with blessings for this life. “Temporal” means belonging to time, as opposed to eternity.
Grumble, complain.
The wicked king of Israel, Ahab’s son, who went into the shipbuilding with Jehoshaphat ([[2Chr.20.35-2Chr.20.36|2 Chronicles 20:35–36]]).
Discipline, correction.
Like two different animals forced to pull under one yoke. Paul uses the picture for close partnerships between believers and unbelievers ([[2Cor.6.14|2 Corinthians 6:14]]).
[[Heb.7.26|Hebrews 7:26]], describing Christ, “separate from sinners.”

modern:
The axe head seemed hopelessly lost. And since it was borrowed, the honor of the band of prophets was at risk, and with it the name of their God. But against all expectation, the iron was made to rise from the bottom of the river and float, because things impossible with man are possible with God.

Only a few years ago I knew a man in Christ who was called to take on a work far beyond his strength. It looked so hard that even the idea of trying it seemed absurd. Yet he was called to it, and his faith rose to the occasion. God honored his faith, unexpected help was sent, and the iron did swim. Another of the Lord’s family was in serious money trouble. He could have paid everything he owed, and much more, if he could have sold a certain part of his property, but he was caught by sudden pressure. He looked for friends to help and found none. But faith led him to the Helper who never fails, and look: the trouble was turned away, his steps were given room, and the iron did swim. A third had a sad case of deep sinfulness to deal with. He had taught, rebuked, warned, invited and prayed, all in vain. Old Adam was too strong for young Melanchthon; the stubborn spirit wouldn’t give in. Then came an agony of prayer, and before long a blessed answer was sent from heaven. The hard heart was broken, and the iron did swim.

Dear reader, what is your desperate case? What heavy matter do you have on your hands this evening? Bring it here. The God of the prophets lives, and lives to help his people. He won’t let you lack any good thing. Believe in the Lord of hosts! Come to him, pleading the name of Jesus, and the iron will swim. You too will see the finger of God working wonders for his people. It will be done for you just as you believe, and once again the iron will swim.

notes.note: A borrowed axe head fell into the Jordan, and at Elisha’s word it floated to the surface ([[2Kgs.6.5-2Kgs.6.6|2 Kings 6:5–6]]).
The “sons of the prophets,” a group learning under Elisha, who were building themselves a new home by the river.
Jesus said, “The things which are impossible with men are possible with God” ([[Luke.18.27|Luke 18:27]]).
Paul’s modest way of describing himself ([[2Cor.12.2|2 Corinthians 12:2]]).
Turned into cash by selling.
He was given room to move. “Thou hast enlarged my steps under me” ([[Ps.18.36|Psalm 18:36]]).
Deep sinfulness; the corruption of human nature.

notes.term: Old Adam was too strong for young Melancthon
notes.note: The young reformer Philip Melanchthon was sure he could persuade anyone to believe, until he found, as he put it, that old Adam was too strong for young Melanchthon. The “old Adam” is the sinful nature we inherit from Adam.
God as commander of the armies of heaven.

notes.term: According to thy faith be it unto thee
notes.note: Jesus’ words as he healed two blind men: “According to your faith be it unto you” ([[Matt.9.29|Matthew 9:29]]).

modern:
By the words “to save” we understand the whole great work of salvation, from the first holy desire right through to being made completely holy. The words pack a great deal into very little; in fact, all of mercy is here in one word. Christ is not only “mighty to save” those who repent; he is able to make people repent. He’ll carry those who believe to heaven, but more than that, he is mighty to give people new hearts and to create faith in them. He is mighty to make someone who hates holiness love it, and to bring someone who despised his name to bow the knee before him.

And that isn’t all it means, because God’s power is just as clear in the work that comes after. A believer’s life is a series of miracles worked by “the Mighty God.” The bush burns, but it isn’t burned up. He is mighty to keep his people holy after he has made them holy, and to keep them in his fear and love until he brings their spiritual life to completion in heaven. Christ’s power doesn’t lie in making a believer and then leaving them to fend for themselves. The One who begins the good work carries it on. The One who gives the first spark of life to the dead soul keeps that divine life going, and makes it stronger, until it bursts every chain of sin and the soul leaps from earth, made perfect in glory.

Believer, here is encouragement. Are you praying for someone you love? Oh, don’t give up praying, because Christ is “mighty to save.” You can’t win back the rebel, but your Lord is Almighty. Take hold of that mighty arm and rouse it to show its strength. Does your own case trouble you? Don’t be afraid, because his strength is enough for you. Whether it’s beginning the work in others or carrying it on in you, Jesus is “mighty to save,” and the best proof is that he has saved *you*. What a mercy, a thousand times over, that you haven’t found him mighty to destroy!

notes.note: The lifelong work of being made holy.
Spurgeon means *multum in parvo*, Latin for “much in little.” “Parro” is a misprint.
Compel; move powerfully.
One of the names of the promised child in [[Isa.9.6|Isaiah 9:6]].
The bush Moses saw burning but not burned up ([[Exod.3.2|Exodus 3:2]]), a picture of God’s people kept alive in the fire.
Completes, brings to its goal.
Fend for himself, manage alone.

notes.term: He who begins the good work
notes.note: From [[Phil.1.6|Philippians 1:6]], “he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.”
Win back.

modern: *Sinking times are praying times* for the Lord’s servants. Peter didn’t pray when he set out on his daring walk, but when he began to sink, his danger made him beg, and his cry, though late, wasn’t too late. In hours of bodily pain and mental anguish, we find ourselves driven to prayer as naturally as a wreck is driven onto the shore by the waves. The fox runs to its hole for protection, the bird flies to the woods for shelter, and in the same way the tested believer hurries to the mercy seat for safety. Heaven’s great harbor of refuge is All-prayer. Thousands of storm-battered ships have found shelter there, and the moment a storm comes up, it’s wise for us to head for it under full sail.

*Short prayers are long enough.* There were only three words in the request Peter gasped out, but they were enough for what he needed. It’s not length we want but strength. A sense of need is a powerful teacher of keeping it short. If our prayers had fewer of pride’s tail feathers and more wing, they’d be all the better. Too many words are to prayer what chaff is to wheat. Precious things come in small packages, and all the real prayer in many a long address could have been said in a request as short as Peter’s.

*Our extremities are the Lord’s opportunities.* The moment a sharp sense of danger forces an anxious cry out of us, the ear of Jesus hears it. With him, ear and heart go together, and his hand doesn’t wait long. We turn to our Master at the last moment, but his quick hand makes up for our delays by acting instantly and effectively. Are we nearly swallowed up by the raging waters of trouble? Then let’s lift up our souls to our Savior, and we can be sure he won’t let us perish. When we can do nothing, Jesus can do everything. Let’s get his powerful help on our side, and all will be well.

notes.note: Daring, risky.
Someone who begs humbly.
Hurries.
The gold lid of the ark of the covenant, where God met with his people ([[Exod.25.22|Exodus 25:22]]); a picture of coming to God in prayer.
From [[Eph.6.18|Ephesians 6:18]], “Praying always with all prayer and supplication.” Spurgeon makes it the name of a harbor.
Too many words.

notes.term: Our extremities are the Lord’s opportunities
notes.note: From the old saying “Man’s extremity is God’s opportunity”: when we’re at the end of our rope, God steps in.
Effective; actually doing what it sets out to do.

modern:
God’s promises were never meant to be tossed aside like scrap paper. He meant them to be used. God’s gold isn’t a miser’s hoard. It’s minted to be spent and traded with. Nothing pleases our Lord more than to see his promises in circulation. He loves to see his children bring them to him and say, “Lord, do as thou hast said.” We glorify God when we plead his promises. Do you think God will be any poorer for giving you the riches he has promised? Do you imagine he’ll be any less holy for giving holiness to you, or any less pure for washing you from your sins? He has said, “Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.”

Faith takes hold of the promise of pardon, and it doesn’t hang back, saying, “This is a precious promise, I wonder if it be true?” It goes straight to the throne with it and pleads, “Lord, here is the promise, ‘Do as thou hast said.’” And our Lord answers, “Be it unto thee even as thou wilt.” When Christians take hold of a promise but don’t bring it to God, they dishonor him. But when they hurry to the throne of grace and cry, “Lord, I have nothing to recommend me but this, ‘Thou hast said it;’” then what they long for will be given. Our heavenly Banker loves to cash his own notes.

Never let the promise rust. Draw the word of promise out of its sheath and use it with holy force. Don’t think God will be bothered by your persistently reminding him of his promises. He loves to hear the loud cries of needy souls. It’s his delight to give good gifts. He is readier to hear than you are to ask. The sun doesn’t get tired of shining, or the fountain of flowing. It’s God’s nature to keep his promises, so go to the throne at once with “Do as thou hast said.”

notes.note: To plead is to ask God earnestly, holding up his own promise as the reason he should act.

notes.term: “Come now, and let us reason together”
“Be it unto thee even as thou wilt”
notes.note: Jesus’ words to the Canaanite woman who wouldn’t stop asking ([[Matt.15.28|Matthew 15:28]]).
God’s throne as a place where sinners are welcome to come for help. “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace” ([[Heb.4.16|Hebrews 4:16]]).
A bank note was once a written promise from the bank to pay the bearer. Spurgeon pictures God’s promises as notes he gladly pays out on.
The sheath for a sword. God’s word is “the sword of the Spirit” ([[Eph.6.17|Ephesians 6:17]]).
Persistently, refusing to give up, like the friend knocking at midnight in [[Luke.11.8|Luke 11:8]].
Give.

modern:
Lying tongues were busy attacking David’s reputation, but he didn’t defend himself. He moved the case to a higher court and pleaded it before the great King himself. Prayer is the safest way to answer words of hatred. The psalmist didn’t pray in a cold-hearted way. He *gave himself* to it, threw his whole heart and soul into it, straining every sinew and muscle, the way Jacob did when he wrestled with the angel. That’s how, and the only way, any of us will succeed at the throne of grace. A shadow has no power, because there’s nothing solid in it. In the same way, a prayer the person praying isn’t fully present in, with agonizing earnestness and fierce desire, does nothing at all, because it lacks the very thing that would give it force. “Fervent prayer,” says an old preacher, “like a cannon planted at the gates of heaven, makes them fly open.”

The common fault with most of us is how ready we are to give in to distractions. Our thoughts wander here and there, and we make little progress toward what we want. Like mercury, our mind won’t hold together but rolls off this way and that. What a great evil this is! It harms us, and worse, it insults our God. What would we think of someone who had been granted an audience with a prince, if he played with a feather or chased a fly while he was making his request?

The words of our text also mean keeping at it and never giving up. David didn’t cry out once and then fall back into silence. His holy clamor went on until it brought the blessing down. Prayer mustn’t be something we do now and then, by chance. It must be our daily business, our habit and our calling. As artists give themselves to their models and poets to their study of the classics, so we must devote ourselves to prayer. We must be immersed in prayer as in our natural element, and so pray without ceasing. Lord, teach us to pray in such a way that we win more and more from you in prayer.

notes.note: Succeed, do well.
Tendon; the cords that tie muscle to bone. Jacob’s thigh was put out of joint as he wrestled ([[Gen.32.24-Gen.32.25|Genesis 32:24–25]]).
A humble, earnest request; a prayer.
Useless; achieving nothing.
A divine is a minister or theologian.
Here and there.
Mercury, the liquid metal that breaks into beads and rolls apart.
Loud, insistent crying out.
Prevailing: winning what we ask for. Not today’s sense of “widespread.”
[[1Thess.5.17|1 Thessalonians 5:17]].

modern: This morning let’s hear the Lord Jesus speak to each one of us: “I will *help* thee.” “It’s only a small thing for me, your God, to *help* you. Think what I’ve done already. What! Not help you? Why, I bought you with my blood. What! Not help you? I died for you, and if I’ve done the greater thing, won’t I do the lesser? *Help* you! It’s the least thing I’ll ever do for you. I *have* done more, and I will do more. Before the world began, I chose you. I made the covenant for you. I laid my glory aside and became a man for you. I gave up my life for you. And if I did all that, I’ll surely help you now. In helping you, I’m only giving you what I’ve already bought for you. If you needed a thousand times as much help, I’d give it to you. You need little compared with what I’m ready to give. It’s a lot for you to need, but it’s nothing for me to give. ‘*Help* you?’ Don’t be afraid! If there were an ant at the door of your granary asking for help, it wouldn’t ruin you to give it a handful of your wheat. And you’re nothing but a tiny insect at the door of my all-sufficiency. ‘I will help thee.’”

My soul, isn’t this enough? Do you need more strength than the almighty power of the Trinity, three in one? Do you want more wisdom than is in the Father, more love than shows itself in the Son, or more power than is seen in the working of the Spirit? Bring your empty pitcher here! This well will surely fill it. Hurry, gather up your needs and bring them here: your emptiness, your troubles, your wants. Look, this river of God is full to supply you. What else could you want? Go out, my soul, in this strength of yours. The Eternal God is your helper!

notes.note: A storehouse for grain.
Being enough for everything, lacking nothing.
Being all-powerful.
God as one being in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
The Spirit’s work on our hearts. “Influences” was a common word for it.
From [[Ps.65.9|Psalm 65:9]], “the river of God, which is full of water.”

notes.term: The Eternal God is thine helper
notes.note: An echo of [[Deut.33.27|Deuteronomy 33:27]], “The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms.”
From the hymn “How Firm a Foundation,” built on [[Isa.41.10|Isaiah 41:10]].

modern: Blessed be his name, there was no reason in him for him to die. Neither the sin we’re born with nor any sin he committed had stained him, so death had no claim on him. No one could rightly have taken his life, because he had done no one any wrong. No one could even have killed him by force, unless he had been willing to give himself up to die. But look: one sins, and another suffers. We offended justice, but justice found its satisfaction in him. Rivers of tears, mountains of offerings, seas of the blood of bulls and hills of incense could never have taken sin away. But Jesus was cut off for us, and the cause of God’s anger was cut off at the same time, because sin was put away forever. Here is wisdom, which planned substitution, the sure and quick way of atonement! Here is humility, which brought Messiah the Prince to wear a crown of thorns and die on the cross! Here is love, which led the Redeemer to lay down his life for his enemies!

But it isn’t enough to admire the sight of the innocent bleeding for the guilty. We must make sure we have a share in it. The particular purpose of the Messiah’s death was the salvation of his church. Do we have a part and a place among those he gave his life to ransom? Did the Lord Jesus stand in our place? Are we healed by his wounds? It would be a terrible thing if we were to miss out on a share in his sacrifice. It would be better for us never to have been born. Serious as the question is, it’s a joyful fact that it can be answered clearly and without mistake. To everyone who believes in him, the Lord Jesus is a Savior here and now, and the blood that makes peace with God has been sprinkled on every one of them. Let all who trust in what Messiah’s death has earned be joyful every time they remember him, and let their holy gratitude lead them to give themselves completely to his cause.

notes.note: “Original sin” is the sinful nature everyone inherits from Adam. “Actual sin” is the wrong we ourselves think, say and do.
God’s justice requires sin to be punished. In Christ’s death that demand was fully met, or “satisfied.”
A sweet-smelling resin burned as incense in the temple.
One taking another’s place: here, Christ taking the punishment due to sinners.
Making peace between God and sinners by paying for sin.
Stooping down from a high position, in the good sense: the Son of God lowering himself to serve us.
Christ’s title in [[Dan.9.25|Daniel 9:25]], the verse before the day’s text.
A share, as when an inheritance was divided by casting lots. Peter told Simon the sorcerer, “Thou hast neither part nor lot in this matter” ([[Acts.8.21|Acts 8:21]]).
The marks of a whipping. “With his stripes we are healed” ([[Isa.53.5|Isaiah 53:5]]).
Setting yourself apart for God.

modern:
The apostle John was given the privilege of looking inside the gates of heaven, and as he describes what he saw, he begins, “I looked, and, lo, a Lamb!” This teaches us that the main thing we’ll gaze at in heaven is “the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sins of the world.” Nothing else caught the apostle’s attention as much as the person of that divine Being who has redeemed us by his blood. He is the subject of the songs of all the glorified spirits and holy angels.

Christian, here is joy for you. You’ve looked, and you’ve seen the Lamb. Through your tears your eyes have seen the Lamb of God taking away your sins. So rejoice! In a little while, when your tears have been wiped away, you’ll see the same Lamb *raised up on his throne*. It’s your heart’s joy to have fellowship with Jesus every day. You’ll have the same joy to a greater degree in heaven. You’ll always see him there, and you’ll live with him forever. “I looked, and, lo, a Lamb!” Why, that Lamb is heaven itself, for as good Rutherford says, “Heaven and Christ are the same thing;” to be with Christ is to be in heaven, and to be in heaven is to be with Christ. That prisoner of the Lord writes very sweetly in one of his glowing letters, “O my Lord Jesus Christ, if I could be in heaven without thee, it would be a hell; and if I could be in hell, and have thee still, it would be a heaven to me, for thou art all the heaven I want.” It’s true, isn’t it, Christian? Doesn’t your soul say so?
All you need to make you blessed, supremely blessed, is “to be with Christ.”

notes.note: Mount Zion, the hill of Jerusalem; here, the heavenly city.
Thoughtful, loving gazing.
John the Baptist’s words about Jesus ([[John.1.29|John 1:29]]). The King James reads “the sin of the world.”
Believers who have died and are now with God in heaven.
“God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes” ([[Rev.21.4|Revelation 21:4]]).
Samuel Rutherford (about 1600–1661), a Scottish minister whose letters, many written while he was exiled to Aberdeen for his beliefs, are full of longing for Christ.
From a hymn by Isaac Watts.
Paul’s longing in [[Phil.1.23|Philippians 1:23]], “to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better.”

modern: It was at that hour that David saw Bathsheba. We’re never out of temptation’s reach. At home and away, we’re liable to meet things that draw us toward evil. The morning opens with danger, and evening’s shadows find us still at risk. Those whom God keeps are well kept, but how terrible it is for those who go out into the world, or even dare to walk around their own house, without their armor! People who think they’re safe are more exposed to danger than anyone else. Self-confidence is Sin’s armor-bearer.

David should have been out fighting the Lord’s battles. Instead he stayed behind in Jerusalem and gave himself up to lazy comfort, getting up from his bed in the evening. Idleness and luxury are the devil’s jackals, and they find him plenty of prey. Harmful creatures swarm in still water, and neglected soil soon grows a thick tangle of weeds and briers. Oh, for the compelling love of Jesus to keep us busy and useful! When I see the king of Israel lazily leaving his couch at the end of the day and falling straight into temptation, let me take warning, and post holy watchfulness to guard the door.

Is it possible the king had gone up on his roof to be alone and pray? If so, what a warning it gives us never to count any place, however private, safe from sin! While our hearts are so much like a tinderbox, and sparks so plentiful, we need to take every care, everywhere, to keep a fire from starting. Satan can climb onto rooftops and get into prayer closets. And even if we could shut out that foul fiend, our own sinful desires are enough to ruin us unless grace steps in. Reader, beware of evening temptations. Don’t feel safe. The sun is down, but sin is up. We need a watchman for the night as well as a guard for the day. O blessed Spirit, keep us from all evil tonight. Amen.

notes.note: Evening.
Attractions, enticements.
An old warning: “how terrible it will be for…”
The servant who carried a warrior’s weapons and fought at his side.
Stayed behind. “At the time when kings go forth to battle… David tarried still at Jerusalem” ([[2Sam.11.1|2 Samuel 11:1]]).
Harmful, poisonous.
Compelling. “The love of Christ constraineth us” ([[2Cor.5.14|2 Corinthians 5:14]]).
A box of dry, quick-burning material and a flint for starting a fire.
Small private rooms. Jesus said to pray in your “closet” with the door shut ([[Matt.6.6|Matthew 6:6]]).
The sinful desires still at work in a believer.

modern:
How different the believer’s life in heaven will be from what it is here! Here believers are born to work hard and grow tired, but in the land of the undying, no one ever gets tired. Eager to serve their Master, they find their strength doesn’t match their zeal, and their constant cry is, “Help me to serve thee, O my God.” If they’re really active, they’ll have plenty of work: not too much for their will, but more than their strength can manage. So they’ll cry out, “I am not wearied *of* the labour, but I am wearied *in it*.”

Ah, Christian, the hot day of weariness doesn’t last forever. The sun is nearing the horizon. It will rise again on a brighter day than you’ve ever seen, over a land where they serve God day and night and yet rest from their labors. *Here*, rest is only partial. *There*, it is *perfect*. *Here*, Christians are always unsettled; they feel they haven’t arrived yet. *There*, everyone is at rest. They’ve reached the top of the mountain. They’ve gone up into the arms of their God. They can’t go any higher. Tired worker, worn out with toil, just think of when you’ll rest forever! Can you imagine it? It’s an *eternal* rest, a rest that “remaineth.”

Here, my best joys have “mortal” stamped on their foreheads. My lovely flowers fade. My finest cups are drained to the dregs. My sweetest birds fall to Death’s arrows. My most pleasant days darken into night, and the high tides of my happiness ebb away into sorrow. But *there*, everything is undying. The harp never rusts, the crown never withers, the eye never dims, the voice never falters, the heart never wavers, and the undying soul is completely taken up with infinite delight. Happy day! Happy day, when mortality will be swallowed up by life, and the Eternal Sabbath begins!

notes.note: Heaven, where no one dies.

notes.term: They serve God day and night
notes.note: In heaven the redeemed “serve him day and night in his temple” ([[Rev.7.15|Revelation 7:15]]), yet they “rest from their labours” ([[Rev.14.13|Revelation 14:13]]).
Arrived, reached the goal. Paul writes, “Not as though I had already attained” ([[Phil.3.12|Philippians 3:12]]).
The chest, the place of closest embrace.
Is still to come, waiting for us, from the day’s text ([[Heb.4.9|Hebrews 4:9]]).
The falling of the tide, when the sea draws back.

notes.note: From [[2Cor.5.4|2 Corinthians 5:4]], “that mortality might be swallowed up of life.”
Heaven pictured as an endless day of rest and worship.

modern: The two disciples on the road to Emmaus had a very worthwhile journey. Their companion and teacher was *the best of tutors*, an interpreter one in a thousand, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. The Lord Jesus stooped to become a preacher of the gospel, and he wasn’t ashamed to practice his calling before an audience of two. Nor does he refuse now to become the teacher of even one. Let’s seek the company of so excellent an Instructor, because until he is made wisdom to us, we’ll never be wise enough to be saved.

This unequaled tutor used *the best of books* as his textbook. He could have revealed new truth, but he chose to explain the old. In his perfect knowledge he knew the most instructive way to teach, and by turning straight to Moses and the prophets he showed us that the surest road to wisdom isn’t speculation, or reasoning, or reading human books, but meditating on the Word of God. The quickest way to become spiritually rich in heavenly knowledge is to dig in this diamond mine, to gather pearls from this heavenly sea. When Jesus himself set out to make others rich, he worked in the quarry of Holy Scripture.

The favored pair were led to think about *the best of subjects*, because Jesus spoke about Jesus and explained the things concerning himself. Here the diamond cut the diamond, and what could be finer? The Master of the house unlocked his own doors, led the guests to his table and set his own delicacies on it. The One who hid the treasure in the field guided the searchers to it himself. Naturally our Lord would talk about the sweetest of topics, and he could find none sweeter than his own person and work. We should always search the Word with an eye on these. Oh, for grace to study the Bible with Jesus as both our teacher and our lesson!

notes.note: A village about seven miles from Jerusalem. The risen Jesus walked there with two disciples who didn’t recognize him ([[Luke.24.13-Luke.24.16|Luke 24:13–16]]).
From [[Job.33.23|Job 33:23]], “an interpreter, one among a thousand.”
“In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” ([[Col.2.3|Colossians 2:3]]).
Stooped down kindly from a high position.
Seek out, try to win.

Knowing enough to be saved ([[2Tim.3.15|2 Timothy 3:15]]).
Worked.

modern:
Tell me where you lost Christ’s company, and I’ll tell you the likeliest place to find him. Did you lose Christ in your prayer room by holding back from prayer? Then that’s where you must look for him and find him. Did you lose Christ through sin? You’ll find him no other way than by giving up the sin and, by the Holy Spirit, putting to death the part of you where that desire lives. Did you lose Christ by neglecting the Bible? Then you must find him in the Bible. It’s a true proverb: “Look for a thing where you dropped it, it is there.” So look for Christ where you lost him, because he hasn’t gone away.

But it’s hard work going back for Christ. Bunyan tells us that the pilgrim found the stretch of road back to the Arbor of Ease, where he lost his scroll, the hardest he ever traveled. Going twenty miles forward is easier than going one mile back for the lost proof.

So when you find your Master, take care to cling close to him. But how did you come to lose him? You’d have thought you’d never part with such a precious friend, whose presence is so sweet, whose words are so comforting and whose company is so dear to you! How is it you didn’t keep watch on him every moment, for fear of losing sight of him? Still, since you’ve let him go, what a mercy that you’re looking for him, even though you groan sadly, “O that I knew where I might find him!” Keep looking, because it’s dangerous to be without your Lord. Without Christ you’re like a sheep without its shepherd, like a tree with no water at its roots, like a dry, dead leaf in the storm, cut loose from the tree of life. Look for him with your whole heart, and you’ll find him. Only give yourself completely to the search, and you truly will find him yet, to your joy and gladness.

notes.note: A small private room for prayer ([[Matt.6.6|Matthew 6:6]]).
Holding prayer back. Job is accused of this: “thou… restrainest prayer before God” ([[Job.15.4|Job 15:4]]).
Put to death the part of you that sins. “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth” ([[Col.3.5|Colossians 3:5]]).
Any strong desire, especially a sinful one, not only sexual desire.

In John Bunyan’s *The Pilgrim’s Progress*, Christian falls asleep in a pleasant arbor (a shady resting place) halfway up the Hill Difficulty and loses his roll, the scroll that assures him of his salvation. He has to go back for it.
Proof; here, the roll that assured the pilgrim he was saved.

notes.term: “O that I knew where I might find him!”
notes.note: Job’s cry in [[Job.23.3|Job 23:3]].
Dry and withered.

notes.note: “Ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart” ([[Jer.29.13|Jeremiah 29:13]]).
Truly.

modern:
Last evening we saw him opening the Scriptures. Here we see him opening the understanding. In the first work he has many fellow workers, but in the second he stands alone. Many can bring the Scriptures to the mind, but only the Lord can prepare the mind to receive the Scriptures. Our Lord Jesus is different from every other teacher. They reach the ear, but he teaches the heart. They deal with the outward letter, but he gives an inward taste for the truth, by which we sense its flavor and spirit. The most uneducated people become seasoned scholars in the school of grace when the Lord Jesus, by his Holy Spirit, unfolds the mysteries of the kingdom to them and gives them the divine anointing that lets them see the invisible. How happy we are if the Master has cleared and strengthened our understanding!

How many people of deep learning know nothing of eternal things! They know the killing letter of God’s revelation, but its life-giving spirit they can’t make out. There’s a veil over their hearts that the eyes of fleshly reason can’t see through. That was our own case a little while ago. We who now see were once totally blind. Truth was to us like beauty in the dark, unnoticed and neglected. If it hadn’t been for the love of Jesus, we’d still be in complete ignorance this minute, because without his gracious opening of our understanding we could no more have reached spiritual knowledge than a baby can climb the Pyramids or an ostrich fly to the stars. Jesus’ College is the only one where God’s truth can really be learned. Other schools may teach us what to believe, but only Christ’s can show us how to believe it. Let’s sit at the feet of Jesus and, by earnest prayer, call for his blessed help, so that our dull minds may grow brighter and our weak understanding may take in heavenly things.

notes.note: Taste, flavor.

modern:
As a shepherd, Abel *made his work holy for God’s glory, and offered a sacrifice of blood on his altar, and the Lord had respect to Abel and his offering*. This early picture of our Lord is wonderfully clear and sharp. Like the first streak of light that colors the east at sunrise, it doesn’t show everything, but it plainly shows the great fact that the sun is coming. As we see Abel, a shepherd and yet a priest, offering a sweet-smelling sacrifice to God, we can make out our Lord, who brings before his Father a sacrifice the Lord always accepts. Abel was hated by his brother, hated for no reason, and so was the Savior. The natural, fleshly man hated the accepted man in whom the Spirit of grace lived, and didn’t rest until his blood had been shed. Abel fell, and sprinkled his altar and sacrifice with his own blood, and so he pictures the Lord Jesus, killed by human hatred while he served as a priest before the Lord. “The good Shepherd layeth down his life for the sheep.” Let’s weep over him as we see him slain by the hatred of mankind, staining the horns of his altar with his own blood.

*Abel’s blood speaks.* “The Lord said unto Cain, ‘The voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.’” The blood of Jesus has a mighty voice, and what its winning cry asks for is not vengeance but mercy. It’s precious beyond all preciousness to stand at the altar of our good Shepherd! To see him bleeding there as the slaughtered priest, and then to hear his blood speaking peace to all his flock: peace in our conscience, peace between Jew and Gentile, peace between humanity and its offended Maker, peace all down the ages of eternity for people washed in his blood. Abel is the first shepherd in order of time, but our hearts will always put Jesus first in order of excellence. Great Keeper of the sheep, we the people of your pasture bless you with our whole hearts when we see you slain for us.

notes.note: Made holy, set apart for God.
Looked on with favor, accepted ([[Gen.4.4|Genesis 4:4]]).
A person or event in the Old Testament that pictures Christ ahead of time, like a shadow cast before he came.

Hostility, hatred.

notes.note: Jesus’ words in [[John.10.11|John 10:11]], where the King James reads “giveth his life for the sheep.”
The corner posts of the altar, where the blood of sacrifices was put ([[Lev.4.7|Leviticus 4:7]]).
Hebrews says Jesus’ blood “speaketh better things than that of Abel” ([[Heb.12.24|Hebrews 12:24]]): Abel’s cried out for justice, Christ’s cries out for mercy.

modern:
There are many kinds of vanity. The fool’s cap and bells, the world’s fun, the dance, the music and the drinking cup of the pleasure-seeker: everyone knows these are vanities. They wear their proper name and title on their foreheads. Far more treacherous are things just as empty: the cares of this world and the deceitfulness of riches. A man can chase vanity as truly in the counting-house as in the theater. If he spends his life piling up wealth, he’s passing his days in an empty show. Unless we follow Christ and make our God the great aim of our life, we’re different from the most frivolous people only in appearance.

So there’s clearly great need for the first prayer of our text. “Quicken thou me in thy way.” The psalmist admits he is dull, heavy, sluggish, nearly dead. Perhaps, dear reader, you feel the same. We’re so sluggish that even the best reasons can’t bring us to life, apart from the Lord himself. What! Won’t hell wake me up? Can I think of sinners perishing and still not be roused? Won’t heaven wake me up? Can I think of the reward waiting for the righteous and still be cold? Won’t death wake me up? Can I think of dying and standing before my God and still be lazy in my Master’s service? Won’t Christ’s love move me? Can I think of his dear wounds, can I sit at the foot of his cross, and not be stirred with fervor and zeal? It seems so! No mere thought can bring us to life and zeal. God himself must do it, and that’s why the cry is, “Quicken *thou* me.”

The psalmist pours out his whole soul in fierce pleading. His body and his soul join together in prayer. “Turn away mine eyes,” says the body; “Quicken thou me,” cries the soul. This is a fitting prayer for every day. O Lord, hear it from me tonight.

notes.note: Emptiness, worthlessness: anything that promises much and gives nothing. Not only pride in your looks.
Various, of many kinds.

modern: When Moses sang at the Red Sea, it was his joy to know that all Israel was safe. Not a drop of spray fell from that solid wall until the last of God’s Israel had planted their feet safely on the other side of the flood. Once that was done, the waters at once flowed back into their place, but not until then. Part of that song was, “Thou in thy mercy hast led forth the people which thou hast redeemed.” In the last day, when God’s chosen sing the song of Moses the servant of God and the song of the Lamb, Jesus will be able to boast, “Of all whom thou hast given me, I have lost none.” In heaven there won’t be one empty throne.
Everyone God has chosen, everyone Christ has redeemed, everyone the Spirit has called, everyone who believes in Jesus, will cross the dividing sea safely. We haven’t all landed safely yet:

The front of the army has already reached the shore. We’re marching through the depths, following hard after our Leader into the heart of the sea this very day. Let’s take heart: the rear guard will soon be where the front line already is. The last of the chosen ones will soon have crossed the sea, and then the song of triumph will be heard, when all are safe. But oh, if one were missing! Oh, if one of his chosen family were thrown away! It would make an everlasting discord in the song of the redeemed, and cut the strings of the harps of paradise so that no music could ever be drawn from them again.

notes.note: “Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song” ([[Exod.15.1|Exodus 15:1]]). This edition reads “Then Moses sang,” where “When” is meant.

modern:
Samson was thirsty and ready to die. This problem was completely different from any the hero had faced before. Just getting a drink is nothing like as big a thing as being rescued from a thousand Philistines! But when the thirst was on him, Samson felt that small present difficulty weighed more than the great past one he had been so specially rescued from. It’s very common for God’s people, after they’ve enjoyed a great deliverance, to find a little trouble too much for them. Samson kills a thousand Philistines and piles them up in heaps, and then nearly faints for a little water! Jacob wrestles with God at Peniel and overcomes the Almighty himself, and then goes “halting on his thigh!” Strange that the sinew must shrink every time we win the day! It’s as if the Lord has to teach us how small we are, how nothing we are, to keep us within bounds. Samson boasted very loudly when he said, “I have slain a thousand men.” His boasting throat soon grew hoarse with thirst, and he turned to prayer. God has many ways of humbling his people.

Dear child of God, if after great mercy you’re brought very low, yours isn’t an unusual case. When David had come to the throne of Israel, he said, “I am this day weak, though anointed king.” You must expect to feel weakest when you’re enjoying your greatest triumph. If God has done great rescues for you in the past, your present difficulty is only like Samson’s thirst. The Lord won’t let you faint, or let the daughter of the uncircumcised gloat over you. The road of sorrow is the road to heaven, but there are wells of refreshing water all along the way. So, my tested friend, cheer your heart with Samson’s words, and be sure that God will rescue you before long.

notes.note: Very thirsty.
Relieved, eased.
Where Jacob wrestled all night with God and was given the name Israel. He limped away, “he halted upon his thigh” ([[Gen.32.30-Gen.32.31|Genesis 32:30–31]]).

notes.note: The Philistines. Samson feared he would “fall into the hand of the uncircumcised” ([[Judg.15.18|Judges 15:18]]), and David’s lament says, “lest the daughters of the uncircumcised triumph” ([[2Sam.1.20|2 Samuel 1:20]]).
God split open a hollow place and water came out for Samson ([[Judg.15.19|Judges 15:19]]).
Before long.

modern:
These words are meant to humble God’s people. They’re called God’s vine, but by nature what are they more than anyone else? By God’s goodness they’ve become fruitful, because they’ve been planted in good soil. The Lord has trained them up the walls of his sanctuary, and they bear fruit for his glory. But what are they without their God? What are they without the Spirit’s constant work producing fruit in them?

Believer, learn to throw pride away, since you have no grounds for it. Whatever you are, you have nothing to be proud about. The more you have, the more you owe to God, and you shouldn’t be proud of what makes you a debtor. Think about where you came from. Look back at what you were. Think about what you would have been without God’s grace. Look at yourself as you are now. Doesn’t your conscience accuse you? Don’t your thousand wanderings stand in front of you and tell you that you’re not worthy to be called his child? And if he has made anything of you, doesn’t that teach you that it’s grace that made you different? Great believer, you would have been a great sinner if God hadn’t made you different. You who stand up so bravely for the truth would have stood up just as bravely for error if grace hadn’t taken hold of you.

So don’t be proud, even though you own a large estate, a wide kingdom of grace. Once you didn’t have a single thing to call your own except your sin and misery. Oh, what strange folly, that you, who have borrowed everything, should think of making much of yourself! A poor pensioner living on your Savior’s generosity, someone whose life would die without fresh streams of life from Jesus, and yet proud! Shame on you, silly heart!

notes.note: God asks what the wood of a vine is good for if it bears no fruit. It’s too weak even to make a peg ([[Ezek.15.2-Ezek.15.5|Ezekiel 15:2–5]]).
The Spirit’s work on our hearts.
Producing, giving life to.

notes.term: Unworthy to be called his son

Brave in standing up for the truth ([[Jer.9.3|Jeremiah 9:3]]). Mr. Valiant-for-Truth is also a hero of *The Pilgrim’s Progress*.

modern:
This was Satan’s wicked question about that upright man of long ago. But there are many people today about whom it could fairly be asked, because they love God after a fashion only because he makes them prosper. If things went badly for them, they’d give up all their boasted faith in God. If they can clearly see that the world has gone well for them since the time they suppose they were converted, they’ll love God in their poor, fleshly way. But if they have hard times, they rebel against the Lord. Their love is love of the table, not of the host; love of the cupboard, not of the master of the house.

As for true Christians, they expect to get their reward in the next life, and to endure hardship in this one. The promise of the old covenant is prosperity, but the promise of the new covenant is adversity. Remember Christ’s words: “Every branch in me that beareth fruit”—what? “*He purgeth it, that it may bring forth fruit*.” If you bear fruit, you’ll have to endure trouble. “Alas!” you say, “that is a terrible prospect.” But this trouble produces such precious results that the Christian who goes through it must learn to rejoice in hardships, because as their hardships increase, so their comforts increase through Christ Jesus. You can be sure that if you’re a child of God, you’ll be no stranger to the rod. Sooner or later every bar of gold has to pass through the fire.

Don’t be afraid. Rather, be glad that such fruitful times are in store for you, because in them you’ll be weaned from earth and made ready for heaven. You’ll be set free from clinging to the present and made to long for the eternal things that will so soon be shown to you. When you feel that, as far as the present goes, you really do serve God for nothing, then you’ll rejoice in the infinite reward of the future.

notes.note: For nothing; with nothing to gain.
In a way; after their own fashion.
Of the flesh: the desires of our fallen human nature, not only sexual ones.

modern: Why was Christ chosen out of the people? Speak, my heart, because the heart’s thoughts are best. Wasn’t it so that he could be our brother, tied to us by the blessed bond of shared blood? Oh, what a relationship there is between Christ and the believer! The believer can say, “I have a Brother in heaven. I may be poor, but I have a Brother who is rich, and is a King. Will he let me go without while he’s on his throne? Oh, no! He loves me; he is my Brother.” Believer, wear this blessed thought like a diamond necklace around the neck of your memory. Put it like a gold ring on the finger of your recollection, and use it as the King’s own seal, stamping the requests of your faith with the confidence that they’ll succeed. He is a brother born for hard times, so treat him like one.

Christ was also chosen out of the people so that he would know our needs and feel for us. “He was tempted in all points like as we are, yet without sin.” In all our sorrows we have his sympathy. Temptation, pain, disappointment, weakness, weariness, poverty: he knows them all, because he has felt them all. Remember this, Christian, and let it comfort you. However hard and painful your road, it’s marked by your Savior’s footsteps. And even when you reach the dark valley of the shadow of death and the deep waters of the swelling Jordan, you’ll find his footprints there. Wherever we go, he has gone ahead of us. Every burden we have to carry has once been laid on the shoulders of Immanuel.
Take courage! Royal feet have left a blood-red track on the road, and made the thorny path holy forever.

Let me go without.

modern:
Jesus won’t let his people forget his love. If they were to forget all the love they’ve enjoyed, he would come to them with fresh love. “Do you forget my cross?” he says. “I’ll make you remember it, because at my table I’ll show myself to you again. Do you forget what I did for you in the council chamber of eternity? I’ll remind you of it, because you’ll need a counselor, and you’ll find me ready when you call.” Mothers don’t let their children forget them. If the boy has gone to Australia and doesn’t write home, his mother writes, “Has John forgotten his mother?” Then back comes a sweet letter, which proves the gentle reminder wasn’t in vain. It’s the same with Jesus. He says to us, “Remember me,” and our answer is, “We will remember thy love.”

*We will* remember your love and its matchless history. It’s as old as the glory you had with the Father before the world began. We remember, Jesus, your eternal love, when you became our Guarantor and pledged yourself to us as your promised bride. We remember the love that planned the sacrifice of yourself, the love that thought over that sacrifice until the fullness of time, and longed for the hour when you would say, as the volume of the book had written of you, “Lo, I come.” We remember your love, Jesus, as you showed it to us in your holy life, from the manger in Bethlehem to the garden of Gethsemane. We follow you from the cradle to the grave, because every word and deed of yours was love. And we rejoice in your love, which death didn’t exhaust, your love that shone out in splendor in your resurrection. We remember that burning fire of love that will never let you rest until your chosen ones are all safely home, until Zion is glorified and Jerusalem is settled on her everlasting foundations of light and love in heaven.

notes.note: The Lord’s Supper, where believers remember Christ’s death.

modern: God rescues his people from the snare of the fowler in two senses: *from* it, and *out of* it. First, he rescues them *from* the snare, by not letting them walk into it. And second, if they do get caught in it, he rescues them *out of* it. The first promise is the most precious to some; the second is the best to others.

“He shall deliver thee *from* the snare.” How? Trouble is often the way God rescues us. God knows that our backsliding would soon end in our destruction, and in mercy he sends the rod. We say, “Lord, why is this?” not knowing that our trouble has been the means of saving us from far greater evil. Many people have been saved from ruin this way, by their sorrows and their crosses. These have frightened the birds away from the net. At other times God keeps his people *from* the fowler’s snare by giving them great spiritual strength, so that when they’re tempted to do evil, they say, “How can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”

But what a blessed thing it is that if a believer does, in an evil hour, get caught in the net, God will still bring them out of it! Backslider, be sorry, but don’t despair. Wanderer though you’ve been, listen to what your Redeemer says: “Return, O backsliding children; I will have mercy upon you.” But you say you can’t come back, because you’re a captive. Then listen to the promise: “Surely he shall deliver thee out of the snare of the fowler.” You’ll yet be brought out of every evil you’ve fallen into. And though you’ll never stop being sorry for your ways, the One who has loved you won’t throw you away. He’ll welcome you and give you joy and gladness, so that the bones he has broken may rejoice. No bird of paradise will die in the fowler’s net.

modern:
Her fault wasn’t that she *served*. Being a servant suits every Christian well. “I serve” should be the motto of all the princes of heaven’s royal family. Nor was her fault that she had “*much* serving.” We can’t do too much. Let’s do everything we possibly can. Let head and heart and hands all be busy in the Master’s service. It was no fault of hers that she was busy making a meal for the Master. Happy Martha, to have the chance to host such a blessed guest, and happy too to have the spirit to throw her whole soul so heartily into the work. Her fault was that she grew “*cumbered* with much serving,” so that she forgot *him* and only remembered the serving. She let service crowd out fellowship, and so offered one duty stained with the blood of another.

We ought to be Martha and Mary in one. We should do much service and have much fellowship at the same time. For this we need great grace. It’s easier to serve than to have fellowship. Joshua never grew tired fighting the Amalekites, but Moses, on top of the hill in prayer, needed two helpers to hold up his hands. The more spiritual the activity, the sooner we tire of it. The finest fruits are the hardest to grow, and the most heavenly graces are the hardest to cultivate.

Dear friends, while we don’t neglect outward things, which are good enough in themselves, we must also make sure we enjoy a living, personal fellowship with Jesus. Make sure that sitting at the Savior’s feet isn’t neglected, even under the plausible excuse of doing him service. The first thing for our soul’s health, the first thing for his glory and the first thing for our own usefulness is to keep ourselves in constant fellowship with the Lord Jesus, and to see that the living spirituality of our faith is kept up above everything else in the world.

modern:
And can’t you do this? Are there no mercies you *have experienced*? So what if you’re gloomy now? Can you forget that blessed hour when Jesus met you and said, “Come unto me”? Can’t you remember that thrilling moment when he snapped your shackles, smashed your chains to the ground and said, “I came to break thy bonds and set thee free”? Or if the love of your wedding day with him has been forgotten, there must surely be some precious milestone along the road of life, not quite overgrown with moss, where you can read a happy reminder of his mercy to you. What, did you never have an illness like the one you’re suffering now, and didn’t he make you well? Were you never poor before, and didn’t he supply what you needed? Were you never in a tight spot before, and didn’t he rescue you?

Get up, go to the river of your experience and pull up a few bulrushes, and weave them into a little ark for your infant faith to float safely on the stream. Don’t forget what your God has done for you. Turn over the pages of your book of memories and think about the days of old. Can’t you remember the hill Mizar? Did the Lord never meet you at Hermon? Have you never climbed the Delectable Mountains? Have you never been helped in time of need? No, I know you have. So go back a little way to yesterday’s choice mercies. Even though everything may be dark *now*, light up the lamps of the past. They’ll shine through the darkness, and you’ll trust in the Lord until the day breaks and the shadows flee away. “Remember, O Lord, thy tender mercies and thy lovingkindnesses, for they have been ever of old.”

modern:
When believers are adopted into the Lord’s family, their relationship to old Adam and the law ends at once. But then they’re under a new rule and a new covenant. Believer, you’re God’s child, and your first duty is to obey your heavenly Father. A slavish spirit has nothing to do with you. You’re not a slave, but a child. And now, since you’re a much-loved child, you’re bound to obey your Father’s faintest wish, the slightest hint of his will. Does he tell you to keep a sacred ordinance? You neglect it at your peril, because you’ll be disobeying your Father. Does he command you to seek to be like Jesus? Isn’t it your joy to do so? Does Jesus tell you, “Be ye perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect”? Then you’ll work to be perfect in holiness, not because the law commands it, but because your Savior tells you to.

Does he tell his saints to love one another? Do it, not because the law says, “Love thy neighbour,” but because Jesus says, “If ye love me, keep my commandments;” and this is the commandment he has given you, “that ye love one another.” Are you told to give to the poor? Do it, not because charity is a burden you don’t dare dodge, but because Jesus teaches, “Give to him that asketh of thee.” Does the Word say, “Love God with all your heart”? Look at the commandment and answer, “Ah, commandment, Christ has already fulfilled you. So I don’t need to fulfill you to be saved, but I’m glad to obey you, because God is my Father now and he has a claim on me that I wouldn’t dream of disputing.” May the Holy Spirit make your heart obedient to the compelling power of Christ’s love, so that your prayer will be, “Make me to go in the path of thy commandments; for therein do I delight.” Grace is the mother and nurse of holiness, not the excuse for sin.

modern:
God’s people are his children twice over. They’re his offspring by creation, and they’re his sons and daughters by adoption in Christ. That’s why they have the privilege of calling him “Our Father which art in heaven.” Father! Oh, what a precious word that is! Here is *authority*: “If I be a Father, where is mine honour?” If you’re his children, where is your obedience? Here is *affection* mixed with authority, an authority that doesn’t stir up rebellion. The obedience it asks for is given most cheerfully, and wouldn’t be held back even if it could be. The obedience God’s children give him must be *loving* obedience. Don’t go about God’s service like slaves at their taskmaster’s work. Run in the way of his commands, because it’s your *Father’s* way. Offer your bodies as tools of righteousness, because righteousness is your Father’s will, and *his* will should be his child’s will.

*Father!* Here is a kingly title so sweetly wrapped in love that the King’s crown is forgotten in the King’s face, and his scepter becomes, not a rod of iron, but a silver scepter of mercy. In fact, the scepter seems to be forgotten in the tender hand that holds it. *Father!* Here is honor and love. How great a father’s love is for his children! What friendship can’t do, and mere kindness won’t try, a father’s heart and hand must do for his children. They’re his children, so he must bless them. They’re his children, so he must show himself strong in their defense. If an earthly father watches over his children with constant love and care, how much more does our heavenly Father?

*Abba*, Father! Whoever can say this has made better music than cherubim or seraphim can reach. There is heaven in the depth of that word: *Father!* There is everything I can ask, everything my needs can demand, everything my wishes can desire. I have all in all, to all eternity, when I can say, “Father.”

modern:
We must never stop wondering at the great marvels of our God. It would be very hard to draw a line between holy wonder and *real worship*. When the soul is overwhelmed by the majesty of God’s glory, it worships in silence, even if it doesn’t put that into song, or even speak with bowed head in humble prayer. Our God who became flesh is to be worshiped as “the Wonderful.” That God should take notice of his fallen creature, man, and instead of sweeping him away with the broom of destruction, should himself take on the work of being man’s Redeemer and pay his ransom, is marvelous indeed!

But for each believer, redemption is most marvelous when they look at it in relation to themselves. It’s truly a miracle of grace that Jesus should leave the thrones and royal honors above to suffer shamefully here below *for you*. Let your soul lose itself in wonder, because wonder like this is a very practical emotion. Holy wonder will lead you to *grateful worship* and *heartfelt thanks*. It will make you *watchful in a godly way*: you’ll be afraid to sin against a love like this. Feeling the presence of the mighty God in the gift of his dear Son, you’ll take off your shoes, because the place where you stand is holy ground. At the same time you’ll be moved to *glorious hope*. If Jesus has done such marvelous things for you, you’ll feel that heaven itself isn’t too great to expect. Who can be astonished at anything, once they’ve been astonished at the manger and the cross? What wonder is left after you’ve seen the Savior?

Dear reader, maybe the quiet and solitude of your life mean you can hardly copy the shepherds of Bethlehem, who told what they had seen and heard. But you can at least fill your place in the circle of worshipers before the throne, by wondering at what God has done.

modern:
These words tell us that there is a fullness in Christ. There’s a fullness of real Godhood, for “in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead.” There’s a fullness of perfect humanity, for in him, in a human body, that Godhead was revealed. There’s a fullness of power to atone in his blood, for “the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanseth us from all sin.” There’s a fullness of righteousness in his life that makes us right with God, for “there is therefore now no condemnation to them that are in Christ Jesus.” There’s a fullness of divine power to win in his pleading, for “He is able to save to the uttermost them that come unto God by him; seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.” There’s a fullness of victory in his death, for through death he destroyed the one who had the power of death, that is, the devil. There’s a fullness of power in his resurrection from the dead, for by it “we are begotten again unto a lively hope.” There’s a fullness of triumph in his ascension, for “when he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive, and received gifts for men.”

There’s a fullness of blessings of every kind and shape: a fullness of grace to pardon, grace to give new birth, grace to make holy, grace to keep and grace to make perfect. There’s a fullness at all times: a fullness of comfort in trouble and a fullness of guidance in good times. There’s a fullness of every quality of God, of wisdom, of power, of love, a fullness it would be impossible to survey, let alone explore. “It pleased the Father that in him should *all* fulness dwell.” Oh, what a fullness this must be, that *all* receive from! There must be fullness indeed when the stream is always flowing, and yet the well springs up as freely, richly and fully as ever.

Come, believer, and get all your needs supplied. Ask largely, and you’ll receive largely, because this “fulness” can never run out, and it’s stored where every needy person can reach it: in Jesus, Immanuel, God with us.

modern:
This blessed woman used three powers of her being: her *memory*, because she kept all these things; her *affections*, because she kept them in her heart; and her *intellect*, because she pondered them. So memory, affection and understanding were all at work on the things she had heard. Dear friends, remember what you’ve heard about your Lord Jesus and what he has done for you. Make your heart the golden pot of manna, to keep the memory of the heavenly bread you’ve fed on in days gone by. Let your memory treasure up everything about Christ you’ve felt or known or believed, and then let your fond affections hold *him* tight forever. Love the person of your Lord! Bring out the alabaster box of your heart, even if it’s broken, and let all the precious perfume of your love come streaming over his pierced feet.

Let your mind be busy with the Lord Jesus. Think deeply about what you read. Don’t stop at the surface; dive into the depths. Don’t be like the swallow that touches the stream with its wing, but like the fish that goes down to the deepest water. Stay with your Lord. Don’t let him be like a traveler who stops just for the night, but urge him, saying, “Abide with us, for the day is far spent.” Hold on to him and don’t let him go.

The word “ponder” means to weigh. Get the scales of judgment ready. Oh, but where are the scales that can weigh the Lord Christ? “He taketh up the isles as a very little thing:” who will take *him* up? “He weigheth the mountains in scales”: in what scales will we weigh *him*? So be it: if your understanding can’t take him in, let your affections take hold of him. And if your spirit can’t get its arms around the Lord Jesus by understanding, let it embrace him in the arms of love.

modern:
Don’t you feel in your own soul that perfection isn’t in you? Doesn’t every day teach you that? Every tear that trickles from your eye weeps “imperfection”; every harsh word that comes from your lips mutters “imperfection.” You’ve seen too much of your own heart to dream for a moment of any perfection *in yourself*. But in the middle of this sad awareness of imperfection, here’s comfort for you: you are “perfect in *Christ Jesus*.” In God’s sight you are “complete in him;” *even now* you are “accepted in the Beloved.”

But there’s a second perfection still to come, and it’s certain for all God’s children. Isn’t it a delight to look forward to the time when every stain of sin will be removed from the believer, and they’ll be presented faultless before the throne, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing? Then the church of Christ will be so pure that not even the all-seeing eye of God will find a spot or blemish in her, so holy and so glorious that Hart wasn’t going beyond the truth when he said,

Then we’ll know and taste and feel the happiness of this vast but short sentence, “Complete in Christ.” Not until then will we fully understand the heights and depths of the salvation of Jesus. Doesn’t your heart leap for joy at the thought of it? Black as you are, you’ll be white one day. Filthy as you are, you’ll be clean. Oh, what a marvelous salvation this is! Christ takes a worm and turns it into an angel. Christ takes a black, deformed thing and makes it clean and matchless in his glory, unrivaled in his beauty and fit to be the companion of seraphs. My soul, stop and marvel at this blessed truth of perfection in Christ.

modern:
What did they praise God for? They *praised God for what they had heard*: the good news of great joy that a Savior was born for them. Let’s copy them, and raise our own song of thanks that we’ve heard about Jesus and his salvation. They also *praised God for what they had seen*. That’s where the sweetest music is: what we’ve experienced, what we’ve felt inside, what we’ve made our own, “the things which we have made touching the King.” It isn’t enough to *hear* about Jesus. Just hearing may tune the harp, but the fingers of living faith must make the music. If you’ve seen Jesus with the God-given sight of faith, don’t let cobwebs gather on the harp strings. Wake up your lyre and harp, and sing loud to the praise of sovereign grace.

One thing they praised God for was *how what they had heard matched what they had seen*. Look at the last words: “As it was told unto them.” Haven’t you found the gospel to be in your own life just what the Bible said it would be? Jesus said he’d give you rest. Haven’t you enjoyed the sweetest peace in him? He said you’d have joy and comfort and life through believing in him. Haven’t you received them all? Aren’t his ways ways of pleasantness, and all his paths peace? Surely you can say with the queen of Sheba, “The half has not been told me.” I’ve found Christ sweeter than his servants ever said he was. I looked at the portrait they painted of him, but it was a mere smudge compared with the man himself, because the King in his beauty outshines all imaginable loveliness. Surely what we’ve “*seen*” keeps pace with, no, far outstrips, what we’ve “*heard*.” So let’s glorify and praise God for a Savior so precious and so satisfying.

modern:
On our Christian pilgrimage it’s good, for the most part, to be looking forward. Ahead lies the crown, and onward is the goal. Whether it’s for hope, for joy, for comfort or to stir up our love, the future must, after all, be the great thing faith’s eye is fixed on. Looking into the future, we see sin thrown out, the body of sin and death destroyed, the soul made perfect and fit to share the inheritance of the saints in light. Looking further still, the believer’s enlightened eye can see death’s river crossed, the gloomy stream waded through, and the hills of light reached, where the heavenly city stands. Believers see themselves going in through the pearly gates, hailed as more than conquerors, crowned by the hand of Christ, embraced in the arms of Jesus, glorified with him and seated with him on his throne, just as he has overcome and sat down with the Father on his throne.

The thought of this future can well lighten the darkness of the past and the gloom of the present. The joys of heaven will surely make up for the sorrows of earth. Hush, hush, my doubts! Death is only a narrow stream, and you’ll soon have waded across it. Time, how short! Eternity, how long! Death, how brief! Immortality, how endless! I feel as if I’m already eating the grapes of Eshcol and sipping from the well inside the gate. The road is so, so short! I’ll soon be there.

modern:
Blessed be the Lord for another day of mercy, even though I’m tired now from its work. To the Preserver of men I lift my song of thanks. The dove found no rest outside the ark, so she came back to it. And today my soul has learned more fully than ever that there’s no satisfaction to be found in earthly things. God alone can give my spirit rest. My business, my possessions, my family, my accomplishments: these are all well enough in their way, but they can’t satisfy the longings of my undying nature. “Return unto thy rest, O my soul, for the Lord hath dealt bountifully with thee.” It was in the still hour, as the gates of the day were closing, that the dove came back to her master on weary wings. O Lord, help me come back to Jesus like that this evening. She couldn’t bear to spend a night hovering over the restless waste, and I can’t bear to be away from Jesus for even one more hour. He is the rest of my heart, the home of my spirit. She didn’t just land on the roof of the ark; she “came in to him.” In the same way my longing spirit wants to look into the secret of the Lord, to get through to the inside of the truth, to enter what is behind the veil, and really to reach my Beloved. To Jesus I must come. My panting spirit can’t settle for anything less than the nearest and dearest fellowship with him. Blessed Lord Jesus, be with me, show yourself to me and stay with me all night, so that when I wake up I’m still with you.

I notice that the dove brought in her mouth an olive branch she had picked, a reminder of the day gone by and a promise of the days to come. Have I no happy record to bring home? No pledge and down payment of lovingkindness still to come? Yes, my Lord. I bring you my grateful thanks for tender mercies that have been new every morning and fresh every evening. And now, I pray, put out your hand and take your dove into your arms.

modern:
Members of Christ’s church should be people of much prayer, always asking for the anointing of the Holy One to rest on their hearts, so that Christ’s kingdom may come and his “will be done on earth, even as it is in heaven.” But there are times when God seems to show Zion special favor, and those seasons should be to us like “the sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees.” Then we ought to be doubly prayerful and doubly earnest, wrestling at the throne more than we usually do. Then action should be quick and vigorous. The tide is coming in, so now let’s row hard for the shore. Oh, for outpourings of the Spirit like Pentecost, and work like Pentecost!

Christian, there are times in your own life “when thou hearest the sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees.” You have unusual power in prayer. The Spirit of God gives you joy and gladness. The Bible opens up to you. The promises come home to you. You walk in the light of God’s face. You have unusual freedom in your devotions, and closer fellowship with Christ than usual. Now, in joyful times like these, when you hear the “sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees,” is the time to get moving. Now is the time to get rid of any bad habit, while God the Spirit is helping your weakness. Spread your sail, but remember what you sometimes sing:

Only be sure your sail is up. Don’t miss the wind for lack of being ready for it. Ask God’s help, so that you’ll be more earnest in duty when you’re made stronger in faith, more constant in prayer when you have more freedom at the throne, and holier in your way of life while you live closer to Christ.
